# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

input.name: MCP turns your AI from a talker into a doer

values.value: An AI that can only chat is a clever pen pal. Give it MCP and it can actually open the tools you work in — and get things done.
Claude
MCP turns your AI from a talker into a doer
The Model Context Protocol lets AI assistants use real tools. Here is why that changes what they can do for you.

value.markup:
For years, talking to an AI meant copying and pasting. You described your problem, the model described a solution, and you went off to carry it out by hand. The conversation was smart, but the hands were yours.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) changes that. It is an open standard that lets an AI assistant discover and call tools exposed by other software — a database, a ticketing system, a file system, or a CMS — through one consistent interface.

values.value: Tools, connected. Photo by Alina Grubnyak on Unsplash.

value.markup:
From describing to doing

This very blog is a good example. Every document type, every block, every image and every word on this site was created by an AI assistant calling the Umbraco MCP server — no clicking through the backoffice, no hand-written migrations.

  • It inspected the existing document types and data types before changing anything.
  • It modeled the content: element types for blocks, a block grid for the page body.
  • It imported the media and published the content, then read it back to confirm it landed.

The assistant did not need a bespoke plugin for any of that. It simply asked the server what tools were available and used them.

The MCP Blog
Without a standard, every AI-to-tool connection is a custom job. MCP replaces the tangle with a single plug that fits everything.
Claude
One protocol, endless integrations
MCP is a single open standard for connecting AI assistants to tools, replacing a tangle of one-off integrations.

value.markup:
Before USB, every device came with its own cable and its own port. Connecting an AI to your tools has looked much the same: one custom integration per assistant, per tool, each maintained separately and each breaking in its own way.

MCP is the USB port for AI. A tool author writes one MCP server; any MCP-capable assistant can use it. An assistant implements one MCP client; it can talk to every server out there.

values.value: Write the integration once. Use it from every assistant.
The whole point of a standard
Standard connections beat bespoke wiring. Photo by Alexandre Debiève on Unsplash.

value.markup:
Why that is awesome

  • Discoverable. The server tells the assistant what it can do, with typed inputs and descriptions. Nothing is hard-coded into the prompt.
  • Local and private. The Umbraco MCP server runs on your machine, next to your dev site, using a scoped API user.
  • Composable. Add a second server — version control, a browser, a database — and the same assistant can combine them in one task.
  • Future-proof. Swap the assistant or upgrade the tool; the contract in the middle stays the same.

That is a lot of leverage for a small, boring protocol — which is exactly what good standards are.

Before USB, every device came with its own cable and its own port. Connecting an AI to your tools has looked much the same: one custom integration per assistant, per tool, each maintained separately and each breaking in its own way.

MCP is the USB port for AI. A tool author writes one MCP server; any MCP-capable assistant can use it. An assistant implements one MCP client; it can talk to every server out there.

The blog is built and running. The front page and both posts return HTTP 200, with no "Could not render component" fallbacks and the images and CSS loading. I only fetched the pages and never opened them in a browser, so I haven't seen the Tailwind styling.

**To view it:** the site is running now from `dotnet run` in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco`. Open `http://localhost:41576/` or `https://localhost:44317/`. The backoffice login is admin@example.com / 1234567890.

**What I built**
- **Content modeling:**
  - **Block elements:** `heroBlock`, `blogPostListBlock`, `richTextBlock`, `imageBlock` and `quoteBlock`.
  - **Composition:** `seoComposition`, with a meta title and description.
  - **Pages:** `blogHome`, allowed under `siteRoot`, and `blogPost`, each with a block grid property.
  - **Block grid data types:** "Blog Home Block Grid" and "Blog Post Block Grid".
  - **Where they live:** I filed everything in the matching document type folders. Umbraco filed the data types under `/Custom/`.
- **Content:** I created the "MCP Blog" front page under WWW and gave it the domain `/`. It has a hero block and a post-list block. Under it are two published posts:
  - "MCP turns your AI from a talker into a doer"
  - "One protocol, endless integrations"
- **Media:** I imported five Unsplash photos into a "Blog" media folder. The posts' captions credit the photographers of the inline images.
- **Razor and frontend:**
  - **Block rendering:** pages call `GetBlockGridHtmlAsync`. Each block has a `blockgrid/Components/<alias>.cshtml` adapter that maps to a plain model and invokes a ViewComponent. There are no custom renderers or wrapper models.
  - **Files:** the plain models are in `Models/Blocks/` and the ViewComponents in `ViewComponents/`. The component views, `_Layout` and the two page templates are all new.
  - **Styling:** Tailwind styling is in `site.css`, built with `npm install` and `npm run build` in the Frontend project.
- **Everything through MCP:** the document types, data types, templates, media and content were all created through the MCP server, in the order you specified. I wrote no migrations.

**Not verified or worth knowing**
- I haven't seen the page in a browser, so the layout and styling are untested visually.
- `UmbracoContext` is nullable in the list adapter, so I read it with `?.`.
- I changed `Views/_ViewImports.cshtml` to import the project's models namespaces.
- I didn't check that uSync exported the schema to `uSync/`.
- The `blogHome` and `blogPost` types show "allowed in library" as true, which I didn't set deliberately. It's harmless for this demo.
- There is no git repository here, so nothing is committed.
